lines.note: Uni is the sea urchin, directly glossed as sea hedgehogs. The short entry ends on this physical row.

runs.text: Vnjǒ. l, vnxǒ. i, Nenguuo aguru.

lines.note: Unjoo, alternatively unshoo, is explained by nengu wo aguru, paying or presenting the land tax. The alternative visibly begins vnxǒ, restoring the initial v omitted by OCR; Pa- begins pagar below.

runs.text: gar, ou offerecer ao ſenhor, ou dono das terras

lines.note: Gar completes pagar: the payment or offering is made to the lord or owner of the land. The whole row continues the preceding Japanese entry.

runs.text: o rendimento, ou foro dellas. Vt,

lines.note: The object is the revenue or rent of the land. Nenguuo begins the example of paying that revenue, continued on the next row.
Unjoo suru completes nengu wo unjoo suru. The additional noun sense is the revenue itself, matching the Portuguese rendimento.
Unmei denotes fortune or fate. Unmei ga tsuki- starts the example in which that fortune comes to an end.
Ta completes tsukita, followed by the alternative kiwamatta. The printed ta. l, is a verb ending plus the Latin alternative marker, not OCR tail; both expressions are glossed as fortune having ended.

runs.text: Comer que tem calidade quente, ou

lines.note: Unmot names food regarded as having a warming quality. The final t represents a checked Sino-Japanese coda and must not be expanded in the transcription.
The stated quality is the ability to warm the stomach. This completes the thermal description of the food, retaining the printed daquentar and estamago forms.

runs.text: Couſa muito quẽte, ou grande quẽtura.

lines.note: Unnet means strong heat or something very hot. The final Portuguese noun visibly reads quẽtura, with one e carrying the abbreviation tilde, rather than OCR queẽtura.

runs.text: Interior, ou misterio como de algũa eſ-

lines.note: Unnoo denotes the interior or hidden meaning, exemplified by a text or doctrine. The caron and doubled n are retained as printed.
Critura completes escritura, and doutrina supplies the parallel example. Both specify the kind of text whose inner meaning is under discussion.
Unnomi and unomi are alternative forms for swallowing whole. The example unnomini suru uses the first form; the Latin l between headwords is not a Japanese syllable.

runs.text: Engulir algũa couſa como coruo marinho ſem

lines.note: The gloss compares swallowing an object to the way a cormorant does it. Sem introduces the absence of chewing, completed below.
Mastigar completes sem mastigar: swallowing without chewing. The one-word continuation remains a separate body line.

U no koku is the hare hour, here equated with six in the morning. Enlargement places the tilde over the first of the two final a types in manhãa; that occurrence is retained rather than conformed to the reference corpus pattern manhaã.

runs.text: Eſpaço entre o ferro, & hastea da

lines.note: U no kubi, literally the cormorant neck, names the space between a spearhead and its shaft. The definition continues with its customary Japanese finish.

runs.text: lança que os Iapões commũmente cuſtumão vru

lines.note: The Japanese are said commonly to coat this part of the spear. The final vru belongs to vruxar, a Portuguese verb derived from lacquer terminology, and has no visible terminal hyphen.
Xar completes vruxar, with pintar as its explanatory alternative. Both verbs refer to coating or painting the spear part described above.

runs.text: Mezinha que ſe faz do coruo

lines.note: U no kuroyaki is a medicinal preparation made from a cormorant. The worn word Mezinha is supported by its visible letters and the ensuing recipe, replacing OCR Mezis ha.

runs.text: marinho aßado, & torrado em hũa panela, &

lines.note: The cormorant is roasted and toasted in a pot. The beta-shaped double-s type in aßado and the tilde in hũa are retained.

runs.text: feito emcaruão pera fazer ir pera baixo algum

lines.note: It is reduced to charcoal and used, according to this historical gloss, to make an obstruction pass downward. The printed emcaruão remains joined.

runs.text: oßo, ou eſpinha que ſe atraueſou na garganta.

lines.note: The obstruction is a bone or fishbone lodged across the throat. This completes the dictionary’s historical remedy description without adding a modern medical claim.

runs.text: Hũa flor branca aßi chamada que vẽ

lines.note: U no hana is described as a white flower of that name. The scan shows aßi, not OCR aßs; the time of flowering follows on the next row.

The printed month name reads Xǒguachi, with a caron and the chi ending, rather than OCR Xõgualhi. Although the following flower-rain entry names Xiguachi, that contextual expectation is not used to replace this line’s visibly different month name.
U no hana kudashi is rain of the fourth month, expressed with the embedded Japanese month name Xiguachi. Its spelling remains distinct from the preceding Xǒguachi.
U no hana odoshi names an armour-lacing pattern. The Portuguese tecidura, weaving or lacing, is visible in the scan and corrects OCR tecioura.

runs.text: tem aparencia desta flor a cima dita.

lines.note: The armour lacing is said to resemble the flower mentioned above. A cima remains two printed words, and this row closes that comparison.
U no me, taka no me is the expression for very keen or searching eyes. Co ends the row without a visible hyphen and is completed as como below.
The comparison is to the eyes of a cormorant and a hawk. The Portuguese description completes the compound Japanese expression above.
Unomi is illustrated by unomi wo suru, swallowing whole. The gloss begins engulir sem and continues with the omitted chewing on the next row.
Mastigar completes the definition as swallowing without chewing. This repeats the earlier unnomi sense under its shorter alternative headword.

runs.text: Cabellos de lebre pera pinceis, ou pe-

lines.note: U no ke is hare hair used for brushes, here also described as Japanese pens. The word pe- continues as penas on the following row.
Nas completes penas de Iapão. U no ke no saki hodo mo starts an expression referring to even the tip of a hare hair, a very small degree.
Chigawanu completes the negative expression: not differing or falling short by even that tiny amount. The Portuguese explicitly gives both discrepancy and deficiency.
U no tori is the cormorant, directly identified by coruo marinho. This is a separate bird entry after the hare-hair expression.
Unpat is paraphrased by kumo no binzura, cloud-like temple hair. The Portuguese begins a description of beautiful hair and retains the single l in Cabelos.

runs.text: de ceo muito fermoſos: eſta palaura não ſe vſa

lines.note: The gloss calls the hair very beautiful and of the colour of the sky. It then begins a usage restriction, completed by the reference to the Japanese reading below.
The entry says the Sino-Japanese word is not ordinarily used, but its yomi is. Yomi is an upright Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Unpoo is glossed with Cumomine and takai mine, a high summit. The visibly printed Cumomine is retained without inserting an expected no; the Portuguese definition continues below.

runs.text: do monte. ¶ Item, apud poetas, Nuuens

lines.note: Do monte completes the summit definition. The additional poetic use begins with high clouds, introduced by the Latin apud poetas.

runs.text: altas que aparecem hũas ſobre outras no verão

lines.note: The poetic clouds appear high and piled one above another in summer. The description continues into their comparison with mountains below.
Como montes completes the image of mountain-like clouds. The final upright S labels written usage and is not part of the italic definition.
Unpuu is warm wind, paraphrased by atatakana kaze. The scan supplies a final u with a caron, omitted from OCR Vnp; the final S is an upright written-usage label.
Unpu means fortune, good or bad. Unpuno begins the example whose noun sakai and interpretation follow below.

runs.text: Fim, ou remate em bem, ou em mal.

lines.note: Sakai completes unpu no sakai, the final outcome of fortune for good or ill. The Portuguese reads remate, conclusion, rather than OCR temate.

runs.text: Mouimẽto, & influencias dos ceos de q̃

lines.note: Unki is explained as the movements and influences of the heavens. Mouimẽto, influencias and ceos restore visible letters lost or confused by OCR; de q̃ continues across the column boundary.
Continues the preceding column’s unki definition: human life and the senses depend on those celestial influences. Vn- begins the example on the next physical row.
Unki wo hanuru is equated with kubi wo kiru, cutting off the head. The Portuguese cortar a begins the same explanation and continues below.

runs.text: cabeça, ou tirar avida a alguem.

lines.note: Cabeça completes cutting off the head, with taking someone’s life given as the alternative explanation. The printed avida remains joined.
This separate unki entry means warm weather, paraphrased by atatakana ki. It must not be merged semantically with the preceding celestial-influence entry.
Unkyaku is inferior tea, explained by ashii cha. The explanatory i is followed by a comma in the scan; Vt introduces a modest invitation formula.
Unkyaku wo moosoozu offers the addressee tea with a self-deprecating description. The scan has no pilcrow before the raised capital V; conui- continues as convidar below.
Dar completes convidar: the speaker proposes to entertain the guest with poor tea. The gloss conveys the humble invitation, not a statement that the tea is objectively defective.

runs.text: Eſtar o tempo quente, eu calmoſo.

lines.note: Unkina describes warm or sultry weather. Enlarged inspection supports the printed eu before calmoſo, although ou would be expected in the Portuguese coordination; the anomaly is retained.
Unkini is labeled simply as the adverb corresponding to the preceding warm-weather adjective. No missing Portuguese gloss is supplied.
Unrai is paraphrased by kumo and ikazuchi, cloud and thunder. Tro- begins the Portuguese word for thunder on the following physical row.
Uão completes trouão, thunder. The final upright S marks written usage and remains outside the italic gloss.
Unrin, literally a forest of clouds, describes lofty masses of clouds. Nuuens is visible in the scan; OCR Nuiuens inserts an extra i, while mul- continues below.
Tiplicadas completes multiplicadas, specifying clouds stacked one upon another. The forest metaphor is explained by their multiplicity.

runs.text: Certo Zaxiqui del rey da China.

lines.note: Unryuukaku names a particular royal chamber or pavilion in China. The scan supports Vnriǔcacu, including the caroned u, instead of OCR Vnrificacu; the supplied NINJAL index confirms the lexical identification (Ohshima and Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). Zaxiqui is a Japanese room term embedded in the Portuguese gloss.
Unsoo is explained by hakobi okuru, transporting or forwarding goods. The Portuguese specifies causing them to be carried or brought, continuing below.
De carreto completes the transport gloss. Unsoo baibai no tsu introduces a port used in the movement and trading of merchandise; Por- begins porto below.

runs.text: to que he eſcala de varias mercadorias.

lines.note: To completes porto: the port is a stopping or interchange point for various merchandise. This belongs to the preceding commercial example.

runs.text: Dizem: palaura com que ſe acaba

lines.note: Un un is the quotation-ending expression unnun, here glossed as “they say.” The scan supports Dizem and acaba, replacing OCR Dezem and acala; i is followed by a comma.

runs.text: algũa clauſula de liuro, ou eſcritura.

lines.note: It is used to finish a passage in a book or written text. This explains the function of unnun rather than adding another literal sense.

runs.text: O interior dalgũa couſa: ainda que ſe

lines.note: Unuoo denotes the interior or hidden meaning of something. The entry explicitly distinguishes its written form from its pronunciation in the next row.
Although written as the headword above, the word is pronounced Vnnǒ, with a reference back to that entry. This occurrence of Vnnǒ is embedded in the Portuguese pronunciation explanation.
Unsha is illustrated by goshiki no unsha, a five-coloured royal carriage. The gloss identifies the vehicle and continues with its use and decoration.

runs.text: ſobe o rey toldado de varias ſedas de cores, &

lines.note: The king rides in this carriage, which is canopied with silks of several colours. The Portuguese toldado describes the canopy rather than the passenger.
The carriage is also decorated with various paintings. This closes the vehicle description before the distinct palace-related entry below.
Unshoo is paraphrased by the printed Cumono iye and glossed as above the clouds. The worn final noun is nuuens, not OCR muatemt; iye is retained without substituting the contextually tempting uye.
The phrase is used for the royal palace. This figurative interpretation completes the preceding above-the-clouds entry.
Unyaku is a medicine naturally regarded as warming. The gloss states its traditional thermal quality without specifying an ingredient.
Unei is the shadow of a cloud, paraphrased by kumo no kage. The line ends with a period, not the OCR’s terminal hyphen.
Unzai means good fortune. Unzai ga tsukihateta says that the fortune has completely run out; the Portuguese translation occupies the next row.
The translation states that good fortune or luck has ended. The joined adita is retained as printed.
Unzan is glossed by kumo and yama, clouds and mountains. The row ends mon without a printed hyphen; OCR non loses the initial m of montes.
Tes completes montes. The upright S identifies written usage and is kept outside the italic gloss.
Unzoo is identified only as a kind of food. The brief gloss does not justify supplying a more specific dish name.

O denotes hemp fibre or hemp thread, illustrated by o wo umu, joining or making the fibre into thread. The period after Vo and the italic boundary are restored; Vi- begins the cross-reference vide below.
De completes Vide supra, referring back to the verb entry Vmi, u. The Japanese citation is a cross-reference within the Portuguese apparatus.
Woo is equated with mikado and glossed as king or emperor. The headword’s first V is visibly slanted and remains italic while the caroned o is roman, as in the supplied transcription.

runs.text: Couſa grande: ſempre ſe vſajunto com ou-

lines.note: Oo means great or large and is said always to occur together with another word. The scan supports ſempre rather than OCR lempre; the close printed vſajunto is retained.
Tra completes outra palaura. Oo kaze illustrates the prefix with a strong wind, whose Portuguese vento is divided at the row boundary.
To completes vento; oo nami supplies the second example, large waves. The two compounds illustrate the productive adjective-like prefix.
This o is the honorific particle, illustrated by omeshi. Ar- begins arroz in the explanation of food prepared for a respected person.

runs.text: roz, ou comer feito pera algũa peßoa hõrada.

lines.note: Roz completes arroz. The gloss explains omeshi as rice or prepared food for an honoured person, preserving peßoa and the abbreviated hõrada.
O in yama no o means the end or head of a mountain. The Portuguese begins the definition here and supplies monte on the following row.
Monte completes the definition of yama no o. This one-word continuation is retained separately from the next affirmative response word.

runs.text: Si. Palaura com que ſe mostra conſen-

lines.note: Woo is an affirmative response, glossed by Portuguese Si. The sentence explains that it shows consent; conſen- continues with tir on f541, while the bottom catchword repeats that forthcoming fragment. Si is printed italic with the rest of the Portuguese explanation.
